families.t: sacks, drums, boxes, ingredients, cutting and packing tasks, bulk delivery, mechanical aids, task redesign, repetition and worker involvement
f: Food manufacture includes repetitive handling of sacks, drums, containers, boxes and products.
Cutting, boning, jointing, trussing and evisceration can combine force and repetition.
Bulk storage and delivery can eliminate handling of smaller ingredient containers.
Fork-liftable bulk containers and mechanical lifting aids can reduce manual lifting.
Task assessment should consider load, task, environment and individual capability.
Workstation height, reach, layout and product flow should reduce bending and twisting.
Repetition, pace and recovery time should be addressed through process and work design.
Workers should be involved in trials and review of handling solutions.
families.g: Food handling risk depends on load and container, repetition and pace, posture and reach, temperature and floors, task design, aids and automation, staffing, worker capability and training.

families.s: HSE chilled and frozen food workplace-temperature and entrapment guidance
families.t: reasonable temperature, food hygiene distinction, local chilling, warm workstations, clothing, rest, exposure time, walk-in units and escape
f: Food hygiene law generally regulates food temperature while health and safety law regulates workroom air temperature.
A reasonable workroom temperature can be achieved by chilling the food locally where practicable.
Warm workstations can be provided where the overall room temperature must remain lower.
Suitable protective clothing and warm rest facilities may be required for cold work.
Work organisation should limit exposure duration and allow recovery.
Walk-in chillers and freezers should provide means of escape after accidental entrapment.
Cold-store structural elements and ceilings should be inspected and not overloaded.
Temperature controls should be reviewed with worker symptoms, task demands, airflow and process changes.
families.g: Cold-work risk depends on air temperature and movement, exposure duration, physical effort, clothing and wetness, worker health, rest and warming, entrapment escape and structural condition.

families.s: HSE steel-erection design, sequence and structural-stability guidance
families.t: preconstruction planning, erection sequence, collapse, falls, falling materials, plant, cranes, MEWPs, competence and emergency arrangements
f: Steel erection is a complex rapidly changing process involving substantial materials and significant hazards.
Principal hazards include falls, dropped materials, moving steel, collapse and overturning equipment.
Risks and controls should be selected during pre-construction planning.
A sequential method of erection should be developed with the frame designer or structural engineer.
Specialist contractors should have suitable skills, knowledge, experience and training.
Planning should identify plant, access, connection methods, temporary stability and emergency arrangements.
Manual-handling aids such as cranes and trolleys should reduce lifting and carrying risk.
Site traffic should prevent plant and access equipment being struck and overturned.
families.g: Steel-erection risk depends on design and sequence, temporary stability and connections, height and access, load movement, cranes and MEWPs, traffic, weather, competence and emergency planning.

families.s: HSE construction-site traffic-management and temporary-route guidance
families.t: vehicle-pedestrian separation, route design, reversing, visibility, signs, temporary roads, ground, loading, site rules and coordination
f: Construction vehicle incidents can be prevented through effective management of transport operations.
Traffic risk should be considered throughout the construction process, including design and planning.
Vehicle and pedestrian routes should be separated where practicable.
Temporary routes should reflect changing work areas, ground condition and drainage.
Signs, barriers, temporary signals and controlled crossing points may be needed.
Reversing should be eliminated or reduced and controlled where unavoidable.
Loading, unloading, parking and delivery arrangements should avoid uncontrolled interaction.
Site rules, induction and coordination should communicate the traffic system to workers, visitors and drivers.
families.g: Construction-traffic risk depends on site and route design, changing work areas, vehicles and pedestrians, visibility and reversing, ground and weather, deliveries, signs and barriers, rules and supervision.

families.s: HSE ammonia-refrigeration integrity and emergency-control guidance
families.t: toxicity, flammability, pressure, design, leak detection, ventilation, isolation, plant rooms, emergency drills, maintenance and competence
f: Refrigeration systems have failure modes that should be identified and controlled through design and operation.
Ammonia refrigerant presents toxic, pressure and lower-flammability hazards.
System design should consider refrigerant properties, inventory, pressure, location and occupancy.
Plant rooms need suitable ventilation and arrangements for foreseeable leaks.
Detection and warning systems should support prompt evacuation and response.
Emergency isolation should be possible from a safe location where practicable.
Inspection, maintenance and examination should address pressure integrity, corrosion, valves and protective systems.
Emergency procedures, drills and competent responders should reflect potential release scenarios.
families.g: Ammonia-refrigeration risk depends on inventory, pressure and temperature, system and plant-room design, leak detection and ventilation, isolation, integrity and corrosion, occupancy, emergency plans and competence.
